points.en: Understand the audience: know the particular people you bring the story to, since their wounds, doubts and hopes shape how you tell it.
Understand the text: study the passage patiently, because a hazy grasp produces a hazy sermon and you cannot retell vividly what you have not seen clearly.
Translate the text into the modern context: build the bridge so the hearer feels the ancient event as the first audience did.
Names the five lenses: the text itself, the people, the places, the events and the speakers.
Gives at least one concrete question per lens, such as a person's history or later life, a place's meaning, motives and consequences, or who speaks and what is left unsaid.
Shows how studying one lens could open a sermon, for example a person's future history, a repeated phrase or a telling silence.
Legitimate sanctified imagination colors what Scripture has drawn, rendering sights, sounds and feelings the text implies so the scene lives.
Illegitimate adding contradicts the text, invents events that change its meaning, or puts new words in God's mouth.
Grounds the limit in Scripture's warnings against adding to God's word, and the preacher must keep to the scene God actually gave.
Contemporizing means bringing the ancient scene near into the hearer's own world so he feels it as the first audience did.
Humor can serve by bringing the scene near, as long as it serves the truth and does not mock the sacred or become the point.
Gives an example, such as the spies' good news and bad news or Peter asking where the stumps are.
Retells the crowd's guesses (John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah) as living portraits so the hearer feels why people compared Jesus to each.
The vivid retelling, plus carrying the question to modern voices, makes the question and Peter's confession of Christ real rather than abstract.
Names the modern answers: the Muslim, the Jew, the secularist and the play that never answers.
A story that is only read aloud or reduced to abstract points loses the life that made it a story.
Study must come first: see the scene clearly, understand the audience and plan the translation, since you cannot make others see what you have not seen.
Connects clear study to vivid retelling anchored faithfully to the text.
Names a narrative and identifies who speaks, to whom, why, and what the words reveal.
Draws a sermon angle from a significant silence or a repeated word or phrase.
The sermon material stays rooted in what the text actually says.
Distinguishes coloring the scene with sights, sounds and feelings the text implies (legitimate) from altering it with invented meaning-changing events or words (illegitimate).
His caution is healthy because the limit against adding to Scripture is real, but it should not silence faithful imagination.
Counsel: study closely, render only what the text could bear, and test every added detail against Scripture.
The three steps frame the task: know the audience, understand the text, and translate it into the modern context.
The five lenses (text, people, places, events, speakers) fill the 'understand the text' step until the scene is clear.
Together they take the preacher from a passage to a vivid, faithful sermon aimed at particular hearers.
Names a Bible narrative and sketches a vivid retelling of it.
Sketches a way to contemporize it, such as a modern parallel, contemporary phrase or light humor.
Names one legitimate added detail (implied by the text) and one illegitimate (an invented event or words the text denies).
